row.name: Northcutt-Carter
row.overview: Busy and very popular, one of the climbs in a famous list of North American classics; wayfinding trouble tends to keep most parties on pitch one only.
row.approach: Start at the Bear Lake trailhead and take the trail to Emerald Lake (roughly 1.7 to 1.8 miles one way). Go around the left side of the lake, scramble through talus, and pick up a climbers' trail beneath the wall. The route is on the Third Buttress, the rightmost. Hike snow or talus beneath the face to it; the start is on the face just right of an obvious white rockfall scar. Snow often lingers at the foot of the face early in the season.
row.descent_text: The route tops out at a notch at the top of the Third Buttress, below the true summit. Immediately right of the top, a cairned third class gully leads west; go left of the tower and through the key notch, or you will cliff out. The gully is loose in places, so avoid it with others above. Near the bottom trend uphill and right to keep it gentle, then walk the talus back to the foot of the buttress.

row.name: South Face
row.overview: Quite possibly the park's busiest alpine route, rising the triangular front of a blade-like spire. The wall is broken by a pair of large terraces; past the upper one it thins to a slim blade capped by a small perch.

row.name: D1
row.overview: The earliest line established on the Diamond, and for many the wall's model climb: pumpy, airy, with a bit of questionable stone, though not everyone grants it three stars. A central plumb crack system leads straight to the apex. Down low, 200 to 300 feet of broken, easier-angled ground (5.8 to 5.9) suits moving together. Higher, a 5.10 roof gives way to an overhanging hand crack and a bivy ledge whose bolts are due for replacing; a single decomposing 5.10c lead then reaches cramped Table Ledge, where drips can soak a belayer. There a strenuous boulder problem opens a long lead of steady 5.11. The final 5.8 lead, wet, sometimes iced and runout, may feel hardest. Often dry early, around June.
row.approach: Walk from the Longs Peak Trailhead, reached from Highway 7, up the Longs Peak Trail and then the Chasm Lake Trail, about 4.2 miles and 2,400 ft of gain to the lake. Scramble around the north side of the lake beneath the east face and aim for North Chimney, the hidden gully below the middle of the Diamond with a snow tongue reaching into it; do not mistake the more obvious Field's Chimney for it. North Chimney is loose fourth and low fifth class (about 5.4) with snow early in the season, so keep out from under other parties and expect rockfall. It gains Broadway, the ledge system across the foot of the wall. D1 follows the central crack system; start beneath the D1 pillar near the top of North Chimney, staying a little right on the pillar to keep clear of parties on the Casual Route.
row.descent_text: D1 continues above Table Ledge with a wet 5.11 section and a final runout 5.8 pitch to the top of the Diamond, so the descent is from the top of the wall. From the top of the wall, go to the summit area and take the North Face (old Cables Route) down: third class, with a rappel from the anchors left from the cables (one double-rope or two single-rope rappels). Take care with a heavy pack, since a slip on the north side drops off the far side of the peak. Continue to the Boulderfield and the trail, or follow the ridge toward Mt Lady Washington and drop down a talus slope to the south into the Chasm Lake basin.

row.name: Kor-Ingalls Route
row.overview: An ultra-classic tower route and probably the busiest of all, linking a series of corners that open leftward on the south wall: a crack and squeeze chimney, a jam crack, an off-width in a big dihedral, then a chimney behind a flake. Gear is adequate and it is easier than most desert towers.

row.name: Finger of Fate
row.overview: Pioneer route working through crack lines on the tower's east side and north ridge to an obvious spire perched on the ridge, with an exposed traverse beneath it.
row.approach: Follow the clear trail toward the Titan and loop around the tower to its northeast side, where the line begins. Allow slightly over an hour when hauling a full aid load.
row.best_season: Late spring offers long days for a one-day push, and heat makes the moves harder. Wet rock stays damp for several days following a big storm and is delicate, so let it dry fully.

row.name: East Buttress
row.overview: Moderate climbing from 1954 along the buttress's springtime shadow line, with grades mainly between 5.6 and 5.8. An A0 section on pitch five goes free at 10c, with good protection on slabby rock. Variations higher up suit repeat ascents or passing parties in high season. Snow in the gully can make the early-season descent the crux.

row.name: Regular Northwest Face of Half Dome
row.descent_text: Walk off the top by the cable route and follow the main hiker trail roughly 8 miles down to the valley floor. If the cables are not up for the season, the lowered cables can still be handled hand over hand. Take care on the cables, and expect close to four hours for the hike out.
row.best_season: Summer. Snow often lingers against the cliff foot until early summer, and as the season advances, daylight shrinks and the supply at the foot of the wall dwindles.
